title: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines a retrieval step with an LLM generation step so answers are grounded in real, retrievable source documents instead of relying only on what the model memorized during training. A user question is embedded into a vector, the most similar document chunks are retrieved from a vector store, and those chunks are inserted into the prompt as context before the LLM generates its answer. RAG solves two problems at once: it lets a model answer questions about content it was never trained on (private documents, recent data), and it makes answers auditable, since the retrieved chunks can be shown to the user as citations.

title: What is Kubeflow Pipelines
text: Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) is a platform for building and running reproducible machine learning workflows on Kubernetes. A pipeline is defined as a directed acyclic graph of components, where each component is a containerized step with typed inputs and outputs. KFP handles scheduling each component as a pod, passing artifacts between steps, caching unchanged steps to avoid rerunning them, and giving a visual run history so you can compare parameters and outputs across pipeline executions. It is commonly used to orchestrate data ingestion, feature engineering, training, and evaluation steps as one versioned, repeatable pipeline rather than a collection of manually-run scripts.

title: What is MLflow and its Model Registry
text: MLflow is an open-source platform for tracking machine learning experiments and managing the model lifecycle. Experiment tracking records the parameters, metrics, and artifacts of every training or pipeline run, making runs comparable and reproducible. The Model Registry sits on top of tracking: it stores versioned models with an approval workflow, and lets a team assign an alias such as 'production' or 'staging' to a specific version. Serving code reads the artifact tagged with the 'production' alias rather than hardcoding a specific version number, so promoting a new model version to production is a registry operation, not a code deployment.

title: How Vector Databases Support Semantic Search
text: A vector database stores embeddings, dense numerical vectors that represent the meaning of a piece of text, and lets you query for the vectors closest to a given query vector. Because semantically similar text produces nearby vectors, this enables retrieval by meaning rather than exact keyword match. Most vector databases use an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index, such as HNSW, rather than an exact brute-force search, trading a small amount of recall for a very large gain in query speed at scale. Chroma is a lightweight, embeddable vector database well suited to local development and small-to-medium RAG applications, storing its index as a local persistent directory.

title: Chunking Strategy for RAG Pipelines
text: Before text can be embedded and indexed, documents are split into smaller chunks, since embedding an entire long document as one vector loses too much specific detail to retrieve precisely. Chunk size controls the tradeoff between context and precision: smaller chunks retrieve more precisely but may lose surrounding context, while larger chunks preserve context but dilute the embedding's specificity. Overlap between consecutive chunks (repeating a small portion of text at the boundary) prevents an answer that spans a chunk boundary from being split apart and lost entirely. There is no universally correct chunk size; it should be tuned empirically against a labeled evaluation set for the specific corpus and question types a RAG system needs to answer.

title: Promoting a Model Version to Production
text: Promoting a model to production means assigning it the alias or stage that live serving code actually reads from, so the decision to promote should be gated by an objective comparison against the currently live version, not simply promoting every newly trained version automatically. A typical promotion rule evaluates the new version against a held-out evaluation set, computes a quality metric such as recall or accuracy, and only reassigns the production alias if the new version's metric meets or exceeds the current production version's metric. This keeps the production alias meaningful as a guarantee of quality rather than just a pointer to whatever was most recently trained, and gives an automatic, auditable gate before a new version reaches real users.
